title: Cranmer's hand
hook: after recanting, he recants his recantation and puts the hand that signed into the fire first

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Book of Common Prayer, and a collect that asks God to cleanse the thoughts of our hearts. Did you say it, or read it, before something hard? Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

An old man stands in a church in Oxford, in front of a crowd. He has been in prison a long time. He is the archbishop who gave England its prayer book, and he has since signed papers taking all of it back: accepting the pope, accepting the teaching he once argued against. The crowd has been told what to expect. He will read one more statement of regret, and then he will be burned anyway. He starts to speak. He asks for prayers. He talks about the world, about money, about obeying the queen. And then he reaches the part about his writings, and the speech goes somewhere nobody planned. Today: Cranmer's hand.
screen: `AN OLD MAN IN A CHURCH IN OXFORD.`

segments.voice: Here's how he got there. When Henry's son Edward died, Mary became queen, Catherine of Aragon's daughter. She brought England back to the Catholic faith and back under Rome. Cranmer was the man who had declared her mother's marriage void. He was tried for heresy and kept in prison, and under that pressure he signed recantations. Even so, he was still sent to the stake. The story of the end is told by John Foxe, a Protestant writer who collected the stories of those Mary burned. Foxe has a side, and readers weigh his telling with that in mind. In Foxe's account, Cranmer says the papers he signed were written against the truth in his heart, out of fear of death. And since his hand had offended by writing them, his hand would be punished first. Then, at the stake, Foxe says, he stretched his right hand into the flames and held it there before the fire reached the rest of him. Some readers think of Peter here. On the night Jesus was arrested, Peter sat warming himself at a fire and swore he didn't know him. Then the rooster crowed, and in the King James Bible, "he went out, and wept bitterly." Later, by another fire on a beach, the risen Jesus gave him a way back. Christians remember Cranmer in more than one way. Protestants honor him as a martyr and as the voice of the prayer book. Catholics remember the archbishop who helped break England from Rome. Either way, the story ends with a frightened man who, at the very end, stopped hiding what he thought.

Here's the practice: own one past mistake, plainly. This isn't about punishing yourself. Settle, and breathe. Look at your own hand for a moment. Let it bring something to mind: a message it typed, a thing it signed, a door it shut. Name the mistake in one plain sentence, no excuses attached. Then let your hand rest open on your knee. If you pray, you can hand it to God with your palm open. If you don't, just notice what it's like to say it straight. The bell holds the time.
Cranmer's hand. The hand that signed his recantations, which, in John Foxe's account, he held in the fire first, owning his mistake before he died.
Your line: this hand first. Today, when something goes wrong and part of it is yours, say so first, before anyone else has to. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Anglicans and other Protestants remember Thomas Cranmer as a martyr and as the main shaper of the Book of Common Prayer, and the story of his hand in the fire is often retold from Foxe's Book of Martyrs.

fork.setup: you're Cranmer, brought out to read one last statement of regret before you're burned. what do you do?
options: take back the recantations and say why.
refuse to say anything at all.
fork.reveal: in Foxe's account, he takes them back: they were written out of fear of death, so the hand that wrote them will be punished first.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man who changed his mind to save his life.
what it means: he did sign recantations, then took them back at the end and held the hand that signed them into the fire first.
what a scholar hears: the scene comes to us through John Foxe, a Protestant writer with a side in the story, so readers weigh it as a martyr's account, not a neutral report.

notes: Editor pass: 'by the law of the day, he was condemned anyway' changed to 'he was still sent to the stake' (recanting heretics were usually spared, so the law did not require it); Peter warming himself at a fire sourced to John 18:18 (Matthew 26 has no fire); cut the narrator's verdict 'put the blame exactly where it belonged' and stopped telling both churches what they can see.

Claims rule: no dates or counts (the number of recantations is not stated). The narrative (Mary as Catherine's daughter, Cranmer tried for heresy, condemned despite recanting, burned at Oxford, the speech in St Mary's church) is standard history; the hand scene is attributed to Foxe throughout. Confirm.
The hook's summary of the opening of Cranmer's final speech (asking for prayers, the world, money, obedience to the queen) follows Foxe's account; confirm.
Foxe is paraphrased, not quoted; the 1563/1570 English text exists but is not on the validator's list.
Peter at the fire (Matthew 26) and the charcoal fire on the beach (John 21:9) are summarized; confirm.
Practice explicitly says it is not about punishing yourself; Keeper should confirm the hand imagery feels safe.

Second editor pass: 'Our main account' (an unsourced ranking of sources) changed to 'The story of the end is told by John Foxe'; 'It's hard not to think of Peter' (telling the listener what they think) changed to 'Some readers think of Peter here'.
Audit pass: Foxe framing, Matthew 26:75 and John 18:18 checked; no change.
